notes.summary: Simplification means working out a long expression in the right order and fast: BODMAS, fractions, powers, roots and identities. SSC asks 1 to 2 questions in each tier, and the same skills save time in every other quant topic. The aim is to cancel and spot patterns, not to calculate everything in full.

concepts.title: Order of operations: BODMAS
concepts.body:
Work in this order:

  1. Brackets (innermost first)
  2. Of (means multiply, done before division)
  3. Division and Multiplication, from left to right
  4. Addition and Subtraction, from left to right

Division and multiplication have the same rank, so go left to right: 18 ÷ 3 × 2 = 6 × 2 = 12, not 18 ÷ 6 = 3.

"Of" is stronger than ÷: 48 ÷ 4 of 3 = 48 ÷ 12 = 4. But 48 ÷ 4 × 3 = 12 × 3 = 36.

concepts.title: Brackets and the bar (vinculum)
concepts.body:
Remove brackets in this order: the bar line drawn over numbers first, then ( ), then { }, then [ ].

Example: 30 − [40 − {56 − (25 − 13 − 12)}]
(25 − 13 − 12) = 0
{56 − 0} = 56
[40 − 56] = −16
30 − (−16) = 46

A minus sign before a bracket changes every sign inside it: 20 − (8 − 3) = 20 − 8 + 3 = 15.

concepts.title: Fractions and mixed numbers
concepts.body:
Mixed numbers: add or subtract the whole parts and the fraction parts separately.
3¼ + 2⅓ − 1⅚: wholes 3 + 2 − 1 = 4; fractions ¼ + ⅓ − ⅚ = (3 + 4 − 10)/12 = −¼. Answer 4 − ¼ = 3¾.

Dividing by a fraction: multiply by its reciprocal. 5 ÷ (2/3) = 15/2.

Comparing fractions: cross-multiply. For 5/7 and 7/10: 5 × 10 = 50 and 7 × 7 = 49, so 5/7 is bigger. With many fractions, convert to decimals.

When numerator and denominator differ by the same amount (like 2/3, 3/4, 4/5), the one with bigger numbers is bigger.

Sevenths repeat the digits 142857 starting at a different place: 2/7 = 0.285714..., 3/7 = 0.428571...

Recurring decimals: 0.333... = 3/9, 0.1212... = 12/99, 0.1666... = (16 − 1)/90 = 1/6. Turn them into fractions before adding.

Decimal multiplication: count the total decimal places. 0.3 × 0.02 = 0.006.

concepts.title: Squares, cubes and roots to know
concepts.body:
Learn squares up to 30 and cubes up to 15. Some anchors: 132 = 169, 172 = 289, 192 = 361, 232 = 529, 272 = 729, 412 = 1681; 73 = 343, 113 = 1331, 123 = 1728, 133 = 2197.

Square root of a perfect square: the unit digit gives two choices (for example a square ending in 9 has a root ending in 3 or 7), and the leading digits tell you the range.
√1681: 402 = 1600 and the number ends in 1, so 41.

Decimals: √0.0016 = 0.04 (pairs of decimal places halve). ∛0.008 = 0.2.

Square of a number ending in 5: n52 = n(n + 1) followed by 25. 652 = 6 × 7 = 42, then 25, so 4225.

concepts.body:

Solving for the power: write both sides with the same base, then equate the powers.
9x−1 = 27x−3: 32x−2 = 33x−9, so 2x − 2 = 3x − 9 and x = 7.

If ax = ay then x = y (for a not 0, 1 or −1). If ax = bx with a ≠ b, then x = 0.

concepts.title: Surds and rationalising
concepts.body:
A surd is a root that is not a whole number, like √2 or ∛5.

  • √a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b)
  • Like surds add: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2. Simplify first: √50 + √18 = 5√2 + 3√2 = 8√2.
  • √a + √b is not √(a + b).

Rationalising: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (change the middle sign).
1/(√3 + √2) = (√3 − √2)/(3 − 2) = √3 − √2.
(√5 + √3)/(√5 − √3) = (√5 + √3)2/(5 − 3) = (8 + 2√15)/2 = 4 + √15.

Square root of a + 2√b: find two numbers x and y with x + y = a and xy = b. Then √(a + 2√b) = √x + √y.
√(7 + 2√10): 5 + 2 = 7 and 5 × 2 = 10, so √5 + √2. For a − 2√b the answer is √x − √y (bigger first).

concepts.title: Comparing surds and roots
concepts.body:
Different root orders: raise every number to the LCM of the root orders so that all roots vanish, then compare.
∛2 and ⁴√3: LCM of 3 and 4 is 12. (∛2)12 = 24 = 16 and (⁴√3)12 = 33 = 27. So ⁴√3 is bigger.

Differences of roots: √a − √b = (a − b)/(√a + √b). With the same gap (a − b), the pair with the bigger numbers gives the smaller difference.
So √7 − √5 is less than √5 − √3.

Sums of roots: compare by squaring. (√5 + √6)2 = 11 + 2√30 and (√3 + √8)2 = 11 + 2√24, so √5 + √6 is bigger.

concepts.title: Nested roots: finite and infinite
concepts.body:
Finite nested roots: start from the innermost root and work outward.
√(8 + √1681) = √(8 + 41) = √49 = 7.

Infinite roots: call the whole value y, notice that the same expression appears inside, and solve.

ExpressionValue
√(x + √(x + √(x + ...)))(1 + √(1 + 4x))/2; if x = n(n + 1), the value is n + 1
√(x − √(x − √(x − ...)))(√(1 + 4x) − 1)/2; if x = n(n + 1), the value is n
√(x √(x √(x ...))) for everx
√(x √(x √x)) with n rootsx(1 − 1/2n)

Example: √(12 + √(12 + ...)): 12 = 3 × 4, so the value is 4. √(20 − √(20 − ...)): 20 = 4 × 5, so the value is 4.

concepts.title: Continued (ladder) fractions
concepts.body:
Start at the bottom of the ladder and move up one step at a time.

Example: 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + 1/2))
1 + 1/2 = 3/2
1 ÷ (3/2) = 2/3, so 1 + 2/3 = 5/3
1 ÷ (5/3) = 3/5, so 1 + 3/5 = 8/5

If an unknown sits inside, simplify the ladder from the bottom in terms of the unknown, then solve the equation. Remember 1/(a/b) = b/a.

concepts.title: Identities that simplify calculations
concepts.body:
IdentityUse
a2 − b2 = (a + b)(a − b)5.62 − 4.42 = 10 × 1.2 = 12
(a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2Spot a2 + 2ab + b2 in a numerator
(a + b)2 + (a − b)2 = 2(a2 + b2)Sum of two squares
(a + b)2 − (a − b)2 = 4abProduct from sum and difference
a3 + b3 = (a + b)(a2 − ab + b2)(a3 + b3)/(a2 − ab + b2) = a + b
a3 − b3 = (a − b)(a2 + ab + b2)(a3 − b3)/(a2 + ab + b2) = a − b
a3 + b3 + c3 − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a2 + b2 + c2 − ab − bc − ca)If a + b + c = 0, then a3 + b3 + c3 = 3abc

Example: (0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 + 0.3 × 0.3 × 0.3)/(0.7 × 0.7 − 0.7 × 0.3 + 0.3 × 0.3) = 0.7 + 0.3 = 1.

concepts.title: Approximation and finding the missing value
concepts.body:
Approximation: round each number to a friendly value, then calculate. Recognise hidden fractions: 0.1667 ≈ 1/6, 0.3333 ≈ 1/3, 0.6667 ≈ 2/3, 0.8333 ≈ 5/6, 0.2222 ≈ 2/9, 0.125 = 1/8, 0.0909 ≈ 1/11. Near squares help: √626 ≈ 25, √99 ≈ 10.

Round one number up and another down where you can, so errors cancel. Options are usually far apart, so a close estimate is enough.

Missing value: simplify the known side fully, then solve for the unknown.
x% of 280 = 15% of 240 + 20% of 310: right side = 36 + 62 = 98, so x = 98 × 100/280 = 35.

Percent and fraction swap: x% of y = y% of x. So 18% of 50 = 50% of 18 = 9.

concepts.title: Series that cancel and quick sums

varieties.name: BODMAS and brackets
varieties.how: Clear brackets from the inside out (bar, ( ), { }, [ ]). Then do "of", then ÷ and × from left to right, then + and − from left to right.

varieties.name: Fractions and decimals
varieties.how: Handle whole parts and fraction parts separately, use a common denominator, and turn recurring decimals into fractions before adding.

varieties.name: Powers and indices
varieties.how: Bring every term to the same prime base. Then apply the index laws, or equate the powers if it is an equation.

varieties.name: Surds and square roots
varieties.how: To rationalise, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate. To compare roots of different orders, raise all to the LCM of the orders.

varieties.name: Infinite roots and continued fractions
varieties.how: For an infinite root, set the whole value as y, square, and replace the repeating part by y. Shortcut: if x = n(n + 1), √(x + √(x + ...)) = n + 1 and √(x − √(x − ...)) = n. For ladders, simplify from the bottom up.

steps: Let y = the value. Then y = √(20 − y).
y must be positive, so y = 4. (Shortcut: 20 = 4 × 5, answer 4.)

varieties.name: Using algebraic identities
varieties.how: Give the repeated numbers letters a and b, spot the identity, cancel, then put the numbers back.

steps: Top = a<sup>2</sup> + 2ab + b<sup>2</sup> = (a + b)<sup>2</sup>. Bottom = a<sup>2</sup> − b<sup>2</sup> = (a + b)(a − b).

varieties.name: Approximation and missing value
varieties.how: Replace awkward decimals with nearby fractions or round numbers, cancel, and pick the closest option. For a missing value, simplify the known side and solve.

varieties.name: Series that cancel and quick sums
varieties.how: Rewrite each term as a difference (1/n − 1/(n + 1), or √(n + 1) − √n) so that neighbours cancel. For powers of one number, use the GP sum formula.

tips: Before calculating, look for an identity (a² − b², a³ + b³) or a common factor to cancel.
Learn squares to 30, cubes to 15 and the fraction to decimal table; they turn long work into recall.
For infinite roots, check whether the number is n(n + 1): 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42, 56, 72, 90.
To compare roots of different orders, raise all of them to the LCM of the orders.
In approximation questions, options are far apart, so round boldly.
Use the unit digit of the answer to strike out options quickly.
traps: ÷ and × go left to right: 18 ÷ 3 × 2 is 12, not 3.
A minus sign before a bracket flips every sign inside it.
√a + √b is not √(a + b), and (a + b)² is not a² + b².
An infinite root has a positive value; reject the negative root of the quadratic.

formulas.name: Root of a + 2√b
formulas.expr: √x + √y where x + y = a and xy = b

formulas.name: Three cubes
formulas.expr: If a + b + c = 0, a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc

questions.q: Which of the following is the largest: √3, ∛4, ⁴√6?
questions.solution:
LCM of 2, 3, 4 = 12. Raise each to the 12th power:
(√3)12 = 36 = 729; (∛4)12 = 44 = 256; (⁴√6)12 = 63 = 216.
Largest is √3.

Let x = √(12 + x).
x2 = 12 + x → x2 − x − 12 = 0 → (x − 4)(x + 3) = 0.
x is positive, so x = 4.
